title: The Sound of the Bīn from the Flute
summary: How to make the flute buzz like a bīn (the snake-charmer's mahuar): cut a second hole near the mouth-hole and cover it with bhojpatra, the thin white membrane inside fresh bamboo. On a transverse flute the hole can go through the cork, with a second cork as an on-off switch; weather affects the membrane.

blocks.text: The Sound of the Bīn in the Flute

blocks.verse:
मुखरन्ध्र समीपे तु छिद्राऽन्यः परिकल्प्यताम्।
बंशजेनैव पत्रेण तमाच्छाद्य निनादयेत्।58।
blocks.text: Near the mouth-hole let another hole be made; cover it with a membrane born of the bamboo itself, and play.

blocks.verse:
मुखरन्ध्रोत्थितो नादो भोजपत्रं प्रकम्पयेत्।
वैचित्र्यं तेन वाद्यस्य ध्वनिः तुम्बुरुवद् भवेत्।59।
blocks.text: The sound rising from the mouth-hole sets the bhojpatra vibrating; this gives the instrument a novel quality, and its tone becomes like Tumburu's.

To change the sound of the flute into a sound like that of the bīn (reed pipe), that is the mahuar, another hole is made near the mukharandhra (mouth-hole), and it is closed by sticking bhojpatra (the thin inner membrane of bamboo) over it with gum. When that membrane vibrates with the sound of the flute, the flute's sound becomes like the bīn. But in this procedure special care must be taken of the weather, because under the effect of heat and cold the kampana (vibration) of the bhojpatra will sometimes be right in the tār saptaka (upper octave) and sometimes right in the mandra saptaka (lower octave). Meeting very dry air, the bhojpatra may also dry out and split. So, according to place and time, wise people can test it and benefit from it. In the āḍī bansī (transverse flute) it can be made, without a separate hole, by making the hole in its kārk (cork) itself, and by closing that with a second cork it can also be opened whenever one wishes; in this way that second cork does the work of a sañcālikā (switch). Just as the jawārī of the bridge works in the sitar, so is the importance of bhojpatra in the flute. So nature has produced bhojpatra inside the bamboo itself. If you split some bamboo while it is still fresh and look, the white membrane stuck to the bamboo inside it, which is especially thin and soft, is what is called bhojpatra. In the transverse flute, a little away from the mouth-hole, [the tube] is closed by fitting a stopper; that is what is called the cork. Some people keep the bamboo's node itself and use it as the stopper, but this does not work very well, so the use of a separate soft material such as rubber, sponge or a bottle cork is what everyone accepts. When putting it in, the bamboo is tied with thick thread; otherwise the bamboo may split.
